questions.q: If the eccentricity of the hyperbola $x^{2}-y^{2} \operatorname{cosec}^{2} \alpha=25$ is $\sqrt{5} times the eccentricity of the ellipse $x^{2} \operatorname{cosec}^{2} \alpha+y^{2}=5$ then \alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution: Eccentrcity of $\frac{x^{2}}{25}-\frac{y^{2}}{25 \sin ^{2} \alpha}=1$ is $\sqrt{1+\sin ^{2} \alpha}$ Eccentricity of $\frac{x^{2}}{5 \sin ^{2} \alpha}+\frac{y^{2}}{5}=1 \quad$ is $\sqrt{1-\sin ^{2} \alpha}$ Given, $\sqrt{1+\sin ^{2} \alpha}=\sqrt{5} \sqrt{1-\sin ^{2} \alpha} \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \sin ^{2} \alpha=\frac{2}{3}$\\ \Rightarrow $\alpha=\sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}=\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{2} \end{array}$

questions.q: The line $2 x+\sqrt{6} y=2$ is a tangent to the curve $x^{2}-2 y^{2}=4$. The point of contact is
questions.solution:
Solving the equation of line and curve, we get
$\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}-2\left\{\frac{2-2 x}{\sqrt{6}}\right\}^{2}=4 \\
\Rightarrow x^{2}-\frac{1}{3} \times 4\left(1+x^{2}-2 x\right)=4 \\
\Rightarrow 3 x^{2}-4-4 x^{2}+8 x=12 \\
\Rightarrow x^{2}-8 x+16=0 \\
\Rightarrow(x-4)^{2}=0 \Rightarrow x=4
\end{array}$
and $\sqrt{6} \cdot y=2-2(4)=-6\Rightarrow y=-\sqrt{6}\therefore$ Point of contact is $(4,-\sqrt{6})$.

questions.q: If $P Q$ is a double ordinate of hyperbola $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1 .$ Such that $O P Q$ is an equilateral triangle, $O$ being the centre of the hyperbola, then the eccentricity ' $e$ ' of the hyperbola satisfies
questions.solution:
Let $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{a} \sec \theta, \mathrm{b} \tan \theta), \mathrm{Q}(\mathrm{a} \sec \theta,-\mathrm{b} \tan \theta)$ be end points of double ordinates and $(0,0)$ is the centre of the hyperbola. So, $\mathrm{PQ}=2 \mathrm{ b} \tan \theta$
$\mathrm{OQ}=\mathrm{OP}=\sqrt{\mathrma^{2} \sec ^{2} \theta+\mathrmb^{2} \tan ^{2} \theta}$ Since, $\mathrm{OQ}=\mathrm{OP}=\mathrm{PQ}\therefore 4 b^{2} \tan ^{2} \theta=a^{2} \sec ^{2} \theta+b^{2} \tan ^{2} \theta\Rightarrow 3 b^{2} \tan ^{2} \theta=a^{2} \sec ^{2} \theta\Rightarrow 3 b^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta=a^{2}\Rightarrow 3 a^{2}\left(e^{2}-1\right) \sin ^{2} \theta=a^{2}\Rightarrow 3\left(e^{2}-1\right) \sin ^{2} \theta=1\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3\left(e^{2}-1\right)}=\sin ^{2} \theta < 1,\left(\because \sin ^{2} \theta < 1\right)\Rightarrow \frac{1}{e^{2}-1} < 3 \Rightarrow e^{2}-1 > \frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow e^{2} > \frac{4}{3}\therefore e > \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $x \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{x}}\right) \mathrm{dy}=\left[\mathrm{y} \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{x}}\right)-\mathrm{x}\right] \mathrm{dx}$ and $y(1)=\frac{\pi}{2}$, then the value of $\cos  \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)is equal to$
questions.solution:
Given : $x \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right) d y=\left[y \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-x\right] d x\Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-x}{x \sin \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$
Put $\frac{y}{x}=z \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=z \cdot 1+x \cdot \frac{d z}{d x}\therefore x \cdot \frac{d z}{d x}+z=\frac{z x \sin z-x}{x \sin z}=z-\operatorname{cosec} z\Rightarrow x \frac{d z}{d x}=-\operatorname{cosec} z \Rightarrow-\sin z d z=\frac{d x}{x}\Rightarrow \cos z=\log x+c\Rightarrow \cos \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)=\log x+c$
But $y(1)=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow x=1, y=\frac{\pi}{2}\therefore \cos \frac{\pi}{2}=\log (1)+\mathrm{c} \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=0\therefore \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{x}}\right)=\log \mathrm{x}$

questions.q: The differential equation of the system of all circles of radius $r$ in the $X Y$ plane is
questions.solution:
The equation of the family of circles of radius $r$ is
$(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=r^{2}$ ...(1)
Where a \& b are arbitrary constants.
Since equation (1) contains two arbitrary constants, we differentiate it two times w.r.t $x \ \text{ and } $ the differential equation will be of second order.
Differentiating (1) w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{array}{l}
2(x-a)+2(y-b) \frac{d y}{d x}=0 \\
\Rightarrow(x-a)+(y-b) \frac{d y}{d x}=0 ...(2)
\end{array}
Differentiating $(2)$ w.r.t. $x$, we get
\begin{array}{l}$1+(y-b) $\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{2}=$0 ...(3) \\\
\Rightarrow(y-b)=-$\frac{1+\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{2}}{\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}} ...($4)
\end{array}
On putting the value of $(y-b)$ in equation (2), we get
$x-a=\frac{\left[1+\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{2}\right] \frac{d y}{d x}}{\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}}$ ...(5)
Substituting the values of $(x-a) \ \text{ and } (x-b)$ in (1), we get
$\begin{array}{l}
{\left[1+\left(\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}\right)^{2}\right]^{2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}\right)^{2}} \\
\left(\frac{\mathrmd^{2} \mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{dx}^{2}}\right)^{2}+\frac{\left[1+\left(\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}\right)^{2}\right]^{2}}{\left(\frac{\mathrmd^{2} \mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{dx}^{2}}\right)^{2}}=\mathrmr^{2} \\
\Rightarrow\left[1+\left(\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}\right)^{2}\right]^{3}=\mathrmr^{2}\left(\frac{\mathrmd^{2} \mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{dx}^{2}}\right)^{2}
\end{array}$

questions.q: \(\mathrm{P}\) is a variable point on the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) whose vertex is \(A(a, 0)\) The locus of the middle point of AP is
questions.solution:
Let \(\left(\mathrm{x}_1, \mathrm{y}_1\right)\) be the mid point of the variable chord AP (where A is fixed while Pvaries) of the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\)
Equation of the chord having \(\left(\mathrm{x}_1, \mathrm{y}_1\right)\) as its mid points is
\(\frac{\mathrm{xx}_1}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{\mathrm{yy}_1}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{x}_1^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{\mathrm{y}_1^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2} \quad\left(\mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{S}_1\right)\)
As it passes through the fixed point \(A(a, 0)\)
\(\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{ax}_1}{\mathrm{a}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{x}_1^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{\mathrm{y}_1^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2} \text{ or } \frac{4 \mathrm{x}_1^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{4 \mathrm{x}_1}{\mathrm{a}}-\frac{4 \mathrm{y}_1^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{4 \mathrm{x}_1^2-4 \mathrm{ax}_1+\mathrm{a}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{4 \mathrm{y}_1^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1 \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{\left(2 \mathrm{x}_1-\mathrm{a}\right)^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{4 \mathrm{y}_1^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1
\end{aligned}\)
Hence locus of \(\left(x_1, y_1\right)\) is \(\frac{(2 x-a)^2}{a^2}-\frac{4 y^2}{b^2}=1\)

questions.q: The combined equation of the asymptotes of the hyperbola $2 x^{2}+5 x y+2 y^{2}+4 x+5 y=0$ is $-$
questions.solution: Let the equation of asymptotes be $2 x^{2}+5 x y+2 y^{2}+4 x+5 y+\lambda=0 \ldots \ldots .(1)$ This equation represents a pair of straight lines, $\begin{array}{l} \therefore$ a b c+2 f g h-a f^{2}-b g^{2}-c h^{2}=0 \\ \therefore 4 \lambda+25-$\frac{25}{2}-8-\lambda \times \frac{25}{4}=0 \\ \Rightarrow-\frac{9 \lambda}{4}+\frac{9}{2}=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=2 \end{array} Putting the value of $\lambda$ in eq. (1), we get 2 x^{2}+5 x y+2 y^{2}+4 x+5 y+2=0$ this is the equation of the asymptotes.

questions.q: If \(e_1\) is the eccentricity of the ellipse \($\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{25}=$1\) and \(e_2\) is the eccentricity of the hyperbola passing through the foci of the ellipse and \(e_1 e_2=1\), then equation of the hyperbola is :
questions.solution:
The eccentricity of \(\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{25}=$1\) is
\$(\begin{aligned}$e_1 & =\sqrt{1-$\frac{16}{25}$}=$\frac{3}{5}$\\
\therefore e_2 & =$\frac{5}{3}$\left(\because$e_1 e_2=1\right)
\end{aligned}\)
\(\Rightarrow\) foci of ellipse \(=(0, $\pm$3)\)
\(\Rightarrow\) Equation of hyperbola is
\(\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}{9}=-$1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Which of the following is INCORRECT for the hyperbola $x^{2}-2 y^{2}-2 x+8 y-1=0$
options: Length of the transverse axis is $2 \sqrt{3}$
Length of the conjugate axis is $2 \sqrt{6}$
questions.solution: The equation of the hyperbola is $x^{2}-2 y^{2}-2 x+8 y-1=0$ or $\quad(x-1)^{2}-2(y-2)^{2}+6=0$ or $\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{-6}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{3}=1$ or $\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{3}-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{6}=1$ or $\quad \frac{Y^{2}}{3}-\frac{X^{2}}{6}=1$ where $X=x-1$ and $Y=y-2\therefore$ The centre $=(0,0)$ in the $\mathrm{X}$ - $\mathrm{Y}$ co-ordinates. $\therefore$ The centre $=(1,2)$ in the $\mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}$ co-ordinates, using $(2)$. If the transverse axis be of length $2 \mathrm{a}$, then a $=\sqrt{3}$, since in the equation (1) the transverse axis is parallel to the y-axis. If the conjugate axis is of length $2 \mathrm{ b}$, then $b=\sqrt{6}$ But $b^{2}=a^{2}\left(e^{2}-1\right)\therefore 6=3\left(\mathrme^{2}-1\right), \quad \therefore \mathrme^{2}=3$ or $\quad \mathrm{e}=\sqrt{3}$ The length of the transverse axis $=2 \sqrt{3}$. The length of the conjugate axis $=2 \sqrt{6}$. Latus rectum $=\frac{2 \mathrm{ b}^{2}}{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{2 \times 6}{\sqrt{3}}=4 \sqrt{3}$

questions.solution:
$F(x+2)=2 F(x)-F(x+1)$...(i)
Putting $x=0$, we get $\begin{array}{l}
F(2)=2 F(0)-F(1) \\
\Rightarrow F(2)=2(2)-3 \\
\quad\{\because F(0)=2, F(1)=3\}
\end{array}$ \Rightarrow F(2)=4-3 \Rightarrow F(2)=1 Putting $ x=1, in $eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned}
F(3) &=2 F(1)-F(2) \\
&=2(3)-1 \quad\{\because F(1)=3, F(2)=1\} \\
\Rightarrow F(3)=5 &
\end{aligned}$ Putting$ x=2, in $eq. (i), we get $\begin{array}{l}
F(4)=2 F(2)-F(3) \\
\quad=2(1)-5 \quad\{\because F(2)=1, F(3)=5\} \\
\Rightarrow F(4)=-3
\end{array}$ Putting$ x=3$, in eq. (i), we get $\begin{array}{l}
F(5)=2 F(3)-F(4) \\
\quad=2(5)+3 \quad\{: F(3)=5, F(4)=-3\} \\
\Rightarrow F(5)=13
